concept: Playing-card coating application curing and compatibility
summary: Source-anchored research for Playing-card coating application curing and compatibility. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: ACTEGA warns that excessive coating slows drying. Adding a thicker layer is therefore not an unconditional remedy for blocking. (low confidence)

ACTEGA treats IR/hot-air dryer settings as application-specific and advises sufficient exhaust air and reduced pile pressure when troubleshooting blocking. These are separate process controls, not a universal cure recipe. (low confidence)

Star Laminators requires dry inks without paraffin waxes, silicones or other slip additives for its UV-coating process. Chicago Laminating also identifies wax/Teflon and incompletely dried ink as adhesion risks. Qualify the actual printed sheet before adopting an offline UV step. (medium confidence)

Duplo requires compatibility testing for all substrates in its application-testing process. EzraCard separately recommends testing a sample for surface friction and shuffle feel. Use both compatibility and handling acceptance for the intended printed-card construction. (medium confidence)

For its Micro coater, Graphic Whizard documents lamp and reflector cleaning when coating smears, and impression-roller and scraper-blade cleaning when coating appears on sheet backs. It separately specifies a tape-pull check for adhesion complaints. Include these diagnosis and maintenance activities when evaluating the coating workflow. (low confidence)

Cork advises washing and drying the aqueous coater blanket or plate when a press stoppage exceeds one minute. This supplier instruction identifies an interruption-related operator task; it does not measure labor for a small card batch. (low confidence)
American Ultraviolet identifies bulb and reflector-liner upkeep as regular maintenance for UV curing systems. Include curing-system maintenance when assessing ownership. (low confidence)

American Ultraviolet presents tape adhesion and scratch testing as common checks for cure completeness. Cork qualifies this advice: tape tests reveal little about cure, and its listed shop tests do not establish absolute cure. Treat these as attributed test limitations when defining sample acceptance. (medium confidence)

PrintPlanet contributor hondarr9 reports that an added UV lamp did not improve coating results on their KM output. This historical operator account shows why added lamp power alone cannot be assumed to solve an unqualified ink/coating combination; it is not a current printer-brand compatibility verdict. (low confidence)

DPS reports supplier guidance that wet versus dry toner dictates coating selection, and that dye, pigment, UV and solvent inkjet systems may need different coatings. A generic digital-print label is insufficient to select a formulation. (low confidence)

Baofengtai markets a water-based playing-card varnish for paper and plastic substrates, with inline, flatbed and double-sided application routes and claimed fanning performance. These are manufacturer descriptions, not an independently demonstrated owner-scale result. (low confidence)

Xindecheng describes a playing-card coating line with automatic feeding, front-side varnishing and IR drying/UV curing, sheet turning, back-side varnishing and drying/curing, then automatic stacking. This is a supplier-described workflow; it does not establish finished-game throughput or suitability for the commissioned game. (low confidence)

Lybrary describes applying its playing-card coating after printing and before cutting, using a hard rubber roller or brayer, with roller cleanup during the manual sequence. This seller-authored DIY account is a trial route, not a measured commercial labor or yield benchmark. (low confidence)

The DIY accounts disagree on Krylon Kamar handling: Lybrary reports inadequate slipperiness, whereas Gobook reports easy shuffling. These attributed results do not establish a universal spray-varnish recipe or independently validated finished-card quality. (low confidence)

For its water-sensitive inkjet receptive coatings, inkAID warns that adding water-based media without first sealing the print can make ink move or blur. This is a specific compatibility counterexample, not proof that every inkjet print needs the same treatment. (low confidence)

In a historical maker account published by World of Playing Cards, Robert Strawn describes hanging printed sheets and spraying them before cutting. This documents a manual application sequence; it does not establish production throughput or commercial shuffle quality. (low confidence)
